content: Pointed arches are one of the most recognisable features of Gothic architecture. Unlike rounded Romanesque arches, they distribute weight more efficiently, allowing buildings to be taller and walls to contain larger windows. Pointed arches are commonly found above doors, windows, arcades, and vaulted ceilings. Besides improving structural strength, they create a strong sense of height and elegance. Visitors can see excellent examples in Westminster Abbey, York Minster, Salisbury Cathedral, and Canterbury Cathedral.

Flying buttresses are stone supports built on the outside of Gothic buildings. They transfer the weight of the roof and upper walls to strong external piers, reducing pressure on the walls. This engineering solution allowed architects to build taller cathedrals with large stained-glass windows. Although they appear decorative, flying buttresses play an important structural role. They can be seen on famous buildings such as Westminster Abbey, York Minster, and Lincoln Cathedral.

Ribbed vaults are arched ceilings made from intersecting stone ribs that support the roof. They became a defining feature of Gothic architecture because they distributed weight efficiently while allowing higher ceilings. The exposed ribs also created decorative patterns that enhanced cathedral interiors. Ribbed vaults are commonly found in churches and cathedrals, including Durham Cathedral, Westminster Abbey, and Gloucester Cathedral. They demonstrate both medieval engineering skill and artistic craftsmanship.

Stained glass windows are decorative windows made from coloured pieces of glass joined by lead strips. They became popular in Gothic churches and cathedrals, where they illustrated religious stories and historical events. Large stained-glass windows were made possible by structural features such as flying buttresses and pointed arches. Sunlight passing through the coloured glass creates vibrant patterns inside the building. Famous examples can be seen in York Minster, Canterbury Cathedral, and King's College Chapel.

Sash windows are a common feature of Georgian architecture. They consist of two movable window panels that slide vertically within the frame. Georgian architects used sash windows to create balanced and symmetrical building facades while providing good ventilation and natural light. Rows of identical sash windows are often seen in Georgian terraces and townhouses. They remain one of the most recognisable features of Britain's historic urban architecture.

Timber framing is a traditional building method that uses large wooden beams to form the main structure of a building. The spaces between the beams were traditionally filled with plaster, brick, or other materials. Decorative black timber with white infill became a distinctive feature of Tudor buildings and later inspired Tudor Revival architecture. Many historic timber-framed buildings can still be seen in towns such as Chester and Stratford-upon-Avon, reflecting Britain's long tradition of skilled craftsmanship.
